title: A compass in an open field
stem:
A compass is placed on a table in an open field, far away from any magnet.

What happens to its needle?
key: A freely turning magnet with no other magnet nearby always comes to rest pointing North–South, N end towards the north.

options.text: It keeps spinning and never stops.
options.pick: The needle is free to turn, so it seems it would keep turning.
options.why: A freely turning magnet always comes to rest. It settles pointing North–South.

options.text: It swings, then comes to rest with its N end pointing north.
options.pick: A compass needle is a small magnet that can turn freely. Recall what a freely suspended magnet does when nothing else is near.
options.why: With no magnet nearby, a freely turning magnet comes to rest pointing North–South, with its N end towards the north.

options.text: It comes to rest with its N end pointing south.
options.pick: The needle does settle, and north and south are easy to swap.
options.why: The shaded N end of the needle is the end that points north when nothing else acts on it.

options.text: It stays in whatever direction it was put down.
options.pick: Things on a table usually stay where you put them.
options.why: That is true of a plain plastic needle. A compass needle is a magnet, so it turns by itself until it points North–South.

title: Bringing a N pole close
stem:
The N pole of a bar magnet is brought close to a compass, without touching it.

Which way does the shaded N end of the needle turn?
key: Like poles repel. A N pole pushes the needle's N end away and pulls its S end in.

options.text: Towards the magnet
options.pick: Magnets pull things, so the needle seems to be pulled towards it.
options.why: A magnet attracts the unlike pole and repels the like pole. Here it is the needle's S end that is pulled in.

options.text: It keeps pointing north, because that is what compasses do.
options.pick: Compasses are known for pointing north.
options.why: A compass only rests pointing north when no magnet is near. A magnet close by pushes and pulls the needle's poles and decides where it points.

options.text: Away from the magnet
options.pick: The magnet's N pole and the needle's N end are like poles. Like poles repel.
options.why: Like poles repel, so the N pole pushes the needle's N end away. The needle's S end swings towards the magnet instead.

options.text: It does not move, because the magnet is not touching the compass.
options.pick: Most pushes and pulls you see need something to touch.
options.why: A magnet can push or pull without touching. The needle turns while the magnet is still some distance away.

title: Two magnets that stay together
stem:
Two bar magnets are placed end to end and stay stuck together. The right end of the left magnet is a S pole.

What is the left end of the right magnet?
key: Magnets that hold together are touching at unlike poles.

options.text: A S pole
options.pick: It seems natural for the ends that meet to match.
options.why: Two S poles are like poles, so they would repel and push each other apart. The magnets could not stay stuck together.

options.text: It could be either. You cannot tell.
options.pick: Nothing is labelled on the right magnet, so it seems impossible to know.
options.why: You can tell. The magnets stay together, and touching poles that hold together must be unlike poles.

options.text: That end has no pole.
options.pick: Only one pole was named, so the other end seems to be just the end of a bar.
options.why: Every magnet has two poles, one at each end. There is no magnet with only one pole.

options.text: A N pole
options.pick: They stay together, so the touching poles attract. Only unlike poles attract.
options.why: S must be touching N. Like poles would push the magnets apart.

title: A compass at each end
stem:
Compass P, magnet 1, magnet 2 and compass Q are placed in a straight line, in that order. The two magnets touch and stay together. Compass P's shaded N end points to the right, towards magnet 1.

Which way does compass Q's shaded N end point?
key: Work along the chain one pole at a time: compass → nearest pole → other end → touching pole → other end → next compass.

options.text: To the right, away from magnet 2
options.pick: Work along the line one pole at a time, starting from compass P.
options.why: P's N end is attracted, so magnet 1's left end is S and its right end is N. The magnets hold together, so magnet 2's left end is S and its right end is N. That N pole repels Q's N end, pushing it to the right.

options.text: To the left, towards magnet 2
options.pick: Magnet 2 is right beside compass Q, so the needle seems to be pulled towards it.
options.why: This gets the last step backwards. Magnet 2's right end is N, and N repels the needle's N end. It is the needle's S end that swings towards the magnet.

options.text: Upwards, towards north
options.pick: Compasses point north, so Q seems to point north too.
options.why: A compass rests pointing north only when no magnet is near it. Magnet 2 is right beside compass Q.

options.text: You cannot tell without being told magnet 1's poles.
options.pick: No pole is labelled, so it seems there is nothing to start from.
options.why: Compass P tells you magnet 1's poles: its N end points at the S pole. From there every pole in the line follows.

title: A compass beside a magnet
stem:
A compass is placed on a table, close to a bar magnet. Its needle does not point north.

Which is the best explanation?
key: A magnet pushes and pulls without touching. Close to a compass, the magnet decides where the needle points.

options.text: The compass is faulty. A working compass always points north.
options.pick: Compasses are meant to point north, so one that does not seems broken.
options.why: Nothing is wrong with it. It is doing what a freely turning magnet does when another magnet is close.

options.text: The bar magnet is not touching the compass, so something else must be turning the needle.
options.pick: The magnet is some distance away, so it does not seem to be involved.
options.why: Magnets push and pull without touching. The bar magnet is exactly what is turning the needle.

options.text: The bar magnet's poles push and pull the poles of the needle, so the needle turns to line up with the magnet.
options.pick: Think of the needle as a small magnet. What do two magnets do to each other?
options.why: A magnet can push or pull without touching. Close to the compass, the bar magnet's poles attract and repel the needle's poles, and that decides where the needle points.

options.text: The N pole of the bar magnet pulls the N end of the needle towards it.
options.pick: Magnets pull, so the N pole seems to pull the N end.
options.why: Like poles repel. A N pole pushes the needle's N end away; it pulls the S end towards it.

title: An unmarked magnet
stem:
The ends of a bar magnet are not labelled. When end P is brought close to a compass, the shaded N end of the needle turns away from P.

What is end P?
key: A compass can label an unmarked magnet: its N end is pushed away by a N pole and pulled towards a S pole.

options.text: A S pole
options.pick: The needle's N end moved, so P seems to be its opposite.
options.why: Unlike poles attract. If P were S, it would pull the needle's N end towards it, not push it away.

options.text: A N pole
options.pick: The needle's N end was pushed away. Which pole pushes a N pole away?
options.why: Like poles repel. P pushed the needle's N end away, so P is a N pole.

options.text: You cannot tell. A compass only shows where north is.
options.pick: Compasses are for finding north, not for testing magnets.
options.why: A compass needle is a magnet, so it reacts to any magnet close by. That reaction tells you which pole P is.

options.text: P has no pole. Only one end of a magnet is a pole.
options.pick: If the needle turns away, it seems P is not attracting anything.
options.why: Every magnet has two poles, one at each end. Pushing away is a sign of a pole, not of no pole.

title: A hanging magnet
stem:
A bar magnet is hung from a thread so that it can turn freely. There are no other magnets nearby.

What happens?
key: A freely suspended magnet comes to rest pointing North–South, with its N pole towards the north.

options.text: It keeps turning and never stops.
options.pick: It hangs freely, so nothing seems to stop it turning.
options.why: A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest, pointing North–South.

options.text: It comes to rest pointing east and west.
options.pick: It settles, and any direction seems as likely as another.
options.why: It always settles pointing North–South, not east–west.

options.text: It stays in whatever direction it was hung.
options.pick: A hanging object usually stays still once it stops swinging.
options.why: A plain bar would. A magnet turns by itself until it points North–South.

options.text: It swings, then comes to rest with its N pole pointing north.
options.pick: This is the same as a compass needle: a magnet free to turn.
options.why: A freely suspended bar magnet comes to rest pointing North–South, with its N pole towards the north.

title: Which end is which?
stem:
A bar magnet with unlabelled ends is hung so that it can turn freely, far from other magnets. When it comes to rest, end X points north.

Which statement is correct?
key: The end of a freely suspended magnet that points north is its N pole. The other end is its S pole.

options.text: End X is the S pole.
options.pick: North and south are easy to swap round.
options.why: The N pole is the end that points north. End X points north, so it is the N pole.

options.text: End X is the N pole.
options.pick: Recall which pole of a freely suspended magnet points north.
options.why: A freely suspended magnet rests with its N pole pointing north, so end X is the N pole.

options.text: End X is not a pole. Only the other end is a pole.
options.pick: Only one end was mentioned, so it seems only one end matters.
options.why: Every magnet has two poles, one at each end. End X is one of them.

options.text: You cannot tell, because a hanging magnet can stop in any direction.
options.pick: It could have stopped anywhere, so where it stopped seems to tell you nothing.
options.why: A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest North–South, so where it stops does tell you which end is N.

title: A magnet 3 cm away
stem:
A compass is on a table. A bar magnet is placed 3 cm from it, not touching it.

What happens to the compass needle?
key: A magnet pushes and pulls without touching, and close by it decides where a compass needle points.

options.text: It keeps pointing north, because compasses always point north.
options.pick: A compass is for finding north.
options.why: A compass points north only when no magnet is near. At 3 cm the bar magnet decides where the needle points.

options.text: It does not move, because the magnet is not touching the compass.
options.pick: There is a gap between them, so nothing seems to connect them.
options.why: A magnet can push or pull across a gap. The needle turns even though nothing touches it.

options.text: It turns to line up with the bar magnet.
options.pick: The needle is a small magnet, and another magnet is close to it.
options.why: The bar magnet's poles push and pull the needle's poles without touching, so the needle turns to line up with it.

options.text: It spins round and round and never stops.
options.pick: Two magnets near each other sound like they would make the needle spin.
options.why: The needle turns and then comes to rest, lined up with the bar magnet.

title: Bringing a S pole close
stem:
The S pole of a bar magnet is brought close to a compass.

Which way does the shaded N end of the needle turn?
key: Unlike poles attract: a S pole pulls the needle's N end towards it.

options.text: Towards the magnet
options.pick: The needle's N end and the magnet's S pole are unlike poles.
options.why: Unlike poles attract, so the S pole pulls the needle's N end towards it.

options.text: Away from the magnet
options.pick: Magnets sometimes push, so the needle might be pushed away.
options.why: A S pole pushes away another S pole. It pulls a N pole, so the needle's N end turns towards it.

options.text: It keeps pointing north.
options.pick: That is what a compass usually does.
options.why: With a magnet close by, the magnet decides where the needle points, not north.

options.text: It does not move until the magnet touches the compass.
options.pick: Pushes and pulls usually seem to need contact.
options.why: A magnet pulls without touching. The needle turns before the magnet reaches the compass.

title: Two magnets push apart
stem:
Two bar magnets are placed end to end and they push each other apart. The touching end of the first magnet is a N pole.

What is the touching end of the second magnet?
key: Magnets that push apart are facing each other with like poles.

options.text: A S pole
options.pick: Opposite ends seem to be what you would expect to meet.
options.why: N and S are unlike poles, and unlike poles attract. The magnets would stick together, not push apart.

options.text: It has no pole. The push comes from the first magnet only.
options.pick: Only the first magnet's pole was named, so it seems to be doing all the pushing.
options.why: Every magnet has a pole at each end. Repelling needs two like poles facing each other.

options.text: You cannot tell from this.
options.pick: The second magnet is not labelled at all.
options.why: The push is the clue. Only like poles repel, so the second magnet's end must be N.

options.text: A N pole
options.pick: They push apart. Which poles repel each other?
options.why: Like poles repel. N is pushing against N.

title: Paper clips under a magnet
stem:
A bar magnet is held 1 cm above some steel paper clips, without touching them.

What happens?
key: A magnet attracts magnetic materials such as steel, and it does so without touching.

options.text: Nothing happens until the magnet touches the clips.
options.pick: There is a gap, so the magnet does not seem to reach them.
options.why: A magnet can pull without touching. The clips move across the gap.

options.text: The paper clips are pulled up to the magnet.
options.pick: Steel is a magnetic material, and magnets can pull without touching.
options.why: The magnet attracts the steel clips across the gap, so they jump up to it.

options.text: The paper clips are pushed away from the magnet.
options.pick: Magnets can push as well as pull.
options.why: A magnet only pushes another magnet. Steel paper clips are only ever pulled.

options.text: Only clips under the middle are pulled. The ends of a magnet are not magnetic.
options.pick: The middle of the bar seems like the main part of the magnet.
options.why: A magnet's poles are at its ends. Clips near the ends are pulled too.
